title: Common symptoms of pregnancy
blurb: Give evidence-based advice for nausea, heartburn, constipation, pelvic girdle pain and varicose veins, and spot the symptoms that are not normal.
question: Sadia, 33 weeks, tells her community midwife that her heartburn has not settled with antacids for 2 days. She also has a headache and her face looks puffy. Is this a common symptom of pregnancy, and what should the midwife do?

teach.body: Formally: NICE NG201 section 1.4 sets out interventions for common problems in pregnancy (nausea and vomiting, heartburn, vaginal discharge, pelvic girdle pain), and the NHS gives self-care advice for others such as constipation and varicose veins. In plain English: hormones and a growing baby cause many uncomfortable but normal symptoms. The midwife's job is to offer practical relief and to recognise when a 'common' symptom is really a sign of something serious.
teach.cite: NICE NG201 1.4.1–1.4.15; NHS 'Common health problems in pregnancy'

items.label: pregnant women have nausea, vomiting or both
mild to moderate nausea usually resolves before this
affected by pelvic girdle pain to some degree

teach.caption: RCOG GTG 69; NHS severe vomiting and pelvic pain pages; NICE NG201 1.4.1.

head: Symptom
Advice
rows: Reassure; ginger if she prefers no drugs; antiemetic if she chooses
Diet and lifestyle; consider antacid or alginate
Fibre, water, exercise; review iron with prescriber
Avoid long standing, legs up; stockings ease symptoms
Rest feet up, foot exercises, comfy shoes
teach.caption: Antacids should not be taken within 2 hours of iron or folic acid (NHS).

rows.label: Eating and drinking
values: Cannot keep food or drink down

teach.h: Stepping up care for nausea and vomiting

steps.label: Moderate to severe
steps.sub: consider IV fluids, ideally outpatient; acupressure as adjunct

teach.caption: NICE NG201 1.4.3–1.4.7. Choose an antiemetic with the woman, taking account of her preferences and past experience.

teach.h: When a 'common' symptom is a warning

rows.label: Itching of palms and soles, worse at night
Sudden swelling of face, hands or feet
rows.tag: Possible pre-eclampsia: check BP and urine

rows.label: Heartburn not relieved by antacids, with headache
Discharge with itch, smell or pain passing urine
Vomiting with dehydration or weight loss

teach.note: NHS 'Itching in pregnancy' (2026) and 'Swollen ankles'; NICE NG201 1.4.10.

teach.body: Pelvic girdle pain (sometimes called SPD) is pain over the pubic bone, lower back, perineum or thighs, worse walking, on stairs, standing on one leg or turning in bed. It is not harmful to the baby and most women can still have a vaginal birth. Consider referral to physiotherapy for exercise advice and/or a non-rigid lumbopelvic belt. Advise keeping knees together getting out of a car and noting PGP in her birth plan.
teach.cite: NICE NG201 1.4.15; NHS 'Pelvic pain in pregnancy'

teach.body: Heartburn that does not settle with antacids, plus headache and facial swelling, are warning symptoms of pre-eclampsia, not a common symptom. The midwife checks Sadia's blood pressure and urine for protein. Her BP is 162/112, so she is referred urgently to secondary care to be seen the same day (NICE NG201 1.2.27). The midwife explains why, arranges transport, informs the unit and documents everything.

teach.text: Do not label itching or heartburn 'normal' without asking the next question. Itchy palms and soles without a rash suggest intrahepatic cholestasis, and persistent heartburn with headache or swelling suggests pre-eclampsia.

items: Nausea: reassure (settles before 16 to 20 weeks), ginger or an antiemetic; IV fluids and inpatient care as severity rises.
Heartburn: lifestyle and diet, then antacid or alginate.
Constipation: fibre, water, exercise; iron can worsen it.
Pelvic girdle pain: consider physiotherapy and a non-rigid belt.
Thrush: vaginal imidazole; discharge with itch, smell or pain needs investigating.
Red flags: itchy palms and soles; sudden swelling, headache, visual change or unrelieved heartburn.

summary: You can now give evidence-based first-line advice for the common symptoms of pregnancy and step up care for nausea and vomiting. You can also recognise the warning features of hyperemesis, intrahepatic cholestasis and pre-eclampsia that make a common symptom a deviation from normal.

A.q: Rachel, 9 weeks, has mild nausea and occasional vomiting. She is eating and drinking and would prefer not to take medicines. What should the midwife suggest?
options: Suggest she tries ginger
Arrange outpatient IV fluids
Recommend acupressure wristbands
Start an antiemetic straight away
A.why: NG201 1.4.3: for mild to moderate nausea and vomiting, if she prefers a non-pharmacological option, suggest ginger.

whyNot.1: IV fluids are for moderate to severe nausea and vomiting.
whyNot.2: Acupressure is considered as an adjunct for moderate to severe symptoms.
whyNot.3: She prefers to avoid medicines, and her symptoms are mild.

A.q: Joanne, 28 weeks, has heartburn despite eating smaller meals and avoiding late meals. What does NICE NG201 recommend next?
options: A proton pump inhibitor from the outset
Lying flat for 30 minutes after meals
A trial of an antacid or alginate
Stopping her folic acid supplement
A.why: NG201 1.4.8–1.4.9: give lifestyle and dietary information, and consider a trial of an antacid or alginate.

whyNot.0: NG201 recommends an antacid or alginate trial, not a PPI first.
whyNot.1: Lying flat after meals worsens reflux; propping up the head and shoulders helps.
whyNot.3: Folic acid does not cause heartburn and is important in pregnancy.

A.q: Amy, 26 weeks, has pain over her pubic bone that is worse on stairs and turning in bed. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Advise bed rest until the baby is born
Plan a caesarean birth because of the pain
Fit a rigid pelvic brace for daily wear
Refer to physiotherapy for exercise advice
A.why: NG201 1.4.15: for pregnancy-related pelvic girdle pain, consider physiotherapy referral for exercise advice and/or a non-rigid lumbopelvic belt.

whyNot.0: Keeping active within comfort is advised; bed rest is not recommended.
whyNot.1: Most women with PGP can have a vaginal birth.
whyNot.2: NG201 refers to a non-rigid lumbopelvic belt, not a rigid brace.

B.q: Nina, 11 weeks, has tried two antiemetics from her GP. She feels dizzy, her urine is dark and she cannot keep fluids down. What should be considered?
options: Ginger and small, frequent meals
IV fluids, ideally as an outpatient
Reassurance that it settles by 16 weeks
Stopping all fluids until vomiting eases
B.why: NG201 1.4.6: for moderate to severe nausea and vomiting, consider intravenous fluids, ideally on an outpatient basis (with acupressure as an adjunct); inpatient care if not responding.

whyNot.0: Ginger is for mild to moderate symptoms; she is dehydrated.
whyNot.2: Dehydration needs treatment, not reassurance alone.
whyNot.3: Withholding fluids would worsen her dehydration.

B.q: Bella, 34 weeks, has intense itching of her palms and soles, worse at night, with no rash. What should the midwife advise?
options: Use emollients and review in 2 weeks
Buy antihistamines from a pharmacist
Itching is from the skin stretching
Attend the maternity unit today
B.why: Itchy palms and soles, worse at night, can signal intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy, which needs urgent assessment (NHS 'Itching in pregnancy', 2026).

whyNot.0: Waiting 2 weeks delays diagnosis of possible ICP.
whyNot.1: Self-treatment delays assessment of a possible liver condition.
whyNot.2: This pattern of itching needs investigation, not reassurance.

B.q: Tess, 22 weeks, has an itchy white vaginal discharge typical of thrush. What should be offered?
options: Oral antibiotics for the discharge
Advice that discharge needs no treatment
A vaginal imidazole such as clotrimazole
Douching with a diluted vinegar solution
B.why: NG201 1.4.13: offer vaginal imidazole (such as clotrimazole or econazole) to treat vaginal candidiasis in pregnancy.

whyNot.0: Antibiotics treat bacterial infection, not candida, and can worsen thrush.
whyNot.1: Symptomatic discharge with itching suggests infection needing treatment.
whyNot.3: Douching is not a recommended treatment.

C.q: Sadia, 33 weeks, has heartburn unrelieved by antacids for 2 days, a headache and a puffy face. Her BP is 162/112 mmHg. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Refer to secondary care to be seen the same day
Increase the antacid dose and review in a week
Refer to secondary care to be seen within 48 hours
Advise rest and recheck BP at her 34-week visit
C.why: These are warning symptoms of pre-eclampsia, and BP of 160/110 or higher needs urgent referral to be seen the same day (NG201 1.2.27).

whyNot.1: Unrelieved heartburn with headache and swelling is not simple reflux.
whyNot.2: 48 hours is too slow for severe hypertension.
whyNot.3: Waiting a week with severe hypertension is unsafe.

C.q: Hollie, 20 weeks, takes iron tablets and has had constipation for a fortnight. Which advice is most appropriate?
options: Cut down on fluids to firm the stools
Fibre, water and exercise; review the iron
Stop taking the iron tablets herself
A low-fibre diet to rest the bowel
C.why: NHS advice: eat high-fibre foods, drink plenty of water, exercise regularly, and ask the prescriber whether iron can be stopped or changed, as iron can cause constipation.

whyNot.2: Prescribed iron should be reviewed with the prescriber, not stopped unsupervised.
whyNot.3: A high-fibre diet, not a low-fibre one, helps constipation.

C.q: Ola, 30 weeks, has painful varicose veins in her legs. Which statement about her care is accurate?
options: Stockings will stop new veins forming
They need surgery during pregnancy
Sitting with legs crossed helps flow
Compression stockings may ease symptoms
C.why: NHS advice: compression stockings will not prevent varicose veins but can ease symptoms; avoid long standing, raise the legs and keep active.

whyNot.0: Stockings ease symptoms but do not prevent varicose veins.
whyNot.1: Varicose veins are uncomfortable but not harmful and usually improve after the birth.
whyNot.2: Women are advised not to sit with their legs crossed.

reteach.title: Ease it, then check it
reteach.question: For each common symptom, ask two things: what eases it, and what would make it something other than normal?

blocks.body: Ease it: ginger or an antiemetic for nausea, an antacid or alginate for heartburn, fibre and fluids for constipation, physiotherapy for pelvic girdle pain, stockings and raised legs for varicose veins. Check it: is she dehydrated, itching on palms and soles, newly swollen in the face, headachy or hypertensive? A yes turns comfort advice into escalation.

rows.label: Itching
values: Palms and soles, worse at night

blocks.text: The warning version of a common symptom is managed as a complication: same-day assessment, not self-care.

explain.body: Reassure women that mild to moderate nausea and vomiting are common and likely to resolve before 16 to 20 weeks. Ginger is a non-drug option; antiemetics are chosen with the woman.

test.q: By when are mild to moderate nausea and vomiting likely to resolve, according to NICE NG201?
options: By 8 to 10 weeks
By 28 weeks
Before 16 to 20 weeks
At the birth for most women
test.why: NG201 1.4.1: mild to moderate nausea and vomiting are likely to resolve before 16 to 20 weeks.

whyNot.0: Symptoms often peak around this time rather than resolve.
whyNot.1: Most women are well before 28 weeks.
whyNot.3: Persistence until birth suggests hyperemesis rather than common sickness.

explain.body: Prolonged, severe nausea and vomiting with dehydration (thirst, dizziness, little dark urine) and weight loss. It often needs hospital treatment and raises VTE risk.

test.q: Which feature suggests hyperemesis gravidarum rather than common pregnancy sickness?
options: Dehydration and weight loss
Nausea eased by eating ginger
Morning nausea that settles by noon
Vomiting twice a week with normal intake
test.why: Hyperemesis gravidarum causes prolonged, severe vomiting with dehydration and weight loss (NHS 'Severe vomiting in pregnancy').

whyNot.1: Symptoms that ease with ginger are typical of mild to moderate sickness.
whyNot.2: Nausea that settles during the day is common pregnancy sickness.
whyNot.3: Occasional vomiting with normal intake is not hyperemesis.

explain.body: Gradual swelling of ankles and feet, worse at the end of the day, is common. Sudden swelling of the face, hands or feet, with headache, visual problems or pain under the ribs, may be pre-eclampsia.

test.q: Which type of swelling needs urgent assessment for pre-eclampsia?
options: Gradual ankle swelling by the evening
Sudden swelling of the face and hands
Swollen feet in hot weather
Mild puffiness after long standing
test.why: A sudden increase in swelling of the face, hands or feet can be a sign of pre-eclampsia and needs immediate contact with maternity services (NHS; NG133 1.1.1).

whyNot.0: Gradual evening ankle swelling is common in pregnancy.
whyNot.2: Heat commonly increases dependent swelling of the feet.
whyNot.3: Swelling after standing is a normal dependent effect.

explain.body: Itching is common as skin stretches. Very itchy skin, especially of the palms and soles and worse at night, can be intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy (ICP), which needs urgent assessment and treatment.

test.q: Which pattern of itching should prompt urgent assessment for intrahepatic cholestasis?
options: Itchy stretch marks on the abdomen
An itchy rash in the skin folds
Itchy dry skin over the shins
Itchy palms and soles, worse at night
test.why: Itching of the palms and soles, worse at night, can be a sign of ICP and needs urgent treatment (NHS 'Itching in pregnancy', 2026).

whyNot.0: Itching over stretching abdominal skin is common.
whyNot.1: A rash in skin folds suggests a skin condition, not the typical ICP pattern.
whyNot.2: Dry skin itch is common and managed with emollients.
